items.summary: Every plant starts small and builds itself one part at a time. A seed wakes up, sends down a root, pushes up a shoot, opens leaves and makes its own food from light, water and air. After reading this you can grow a seed and watch each part appear, name the parts of a plant, and explain how a plant makes its food.
items.title: How Do Plants Grow?

items.summary: Rain is old water that has taken a long trip. Water from rivers, lakes and puddles rises into the air, cools, gathers into clouds, and falls back down as drops. After reading this you can explain where rain comes from, name the three steps of the water cycle, and tell the difference between rain, drizzle, snow and hail.
items.title: Where Does Rain Come From?

items.summary: The sky is not blue because of paint or blue water up high. It is blue because sunlight is really a mix of colours, and the tiny bits in the air throw blue light around the whole sky. After reading this you can explain the blue sky, explain a red sunset, and answer the question a friend asks you most often.
items.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?

items.summary: The sky is full of lights, but they are not all the same kind of thing. After reading this, you can say what the Sun, the Moon and a star each are, explain why the Moon seems to change shape, and find real stars in the night sky without a telescope.
items.title: The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars

items.summary: Sleep is not wasted time. While you sleep your body repairs itself, your brain sorts what you learned, and your body clock resets for the next day. After reading this you can explain what sleep is for, say how many hours children need, name what happens to your body and brain at night, and build a bedtime routine that works.
items.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?

items.summary: Brushing feels normal, but teeth are in real danger every single day. After reading this, you can explain what plaque does to a tooth, brush properly, and pick snacks that are kinder to your teeth.
items.title: Why Do We Brush Our Teeth?

items.summary: A bear keeps every pot of honey for himself, and says no to all his friends. Follow him through autumn into the cold winter, when his friends share with him instead. After reading, you can retell the story, use its new words, and tell its lesson about sharing.
items.title: The Bear Who Learned to Share

items.summary: Wren watches the other birds fly and wants to fly too, but she is afraid of falling. Follow her from the branch to the sky. You will learn the three parts of the story, four new words, and the small step that helped her leave the nest.
items.title: The Little Bird Who Wanted to Fly

items.summary: Mai hears a cry in the forest and finds a fox cub stuck in the brambles. Then the animals start to talk. You will meet the three parts of the story, learn four forest words, and find out why the forest only speaks to some people.
items.title: The Magical Forest of Talking Animals

items.summary: A lion catches a small mouse, and the mouse promises to help him one day. Follow the lion and the mouse from the sunny grass to the hunter's net, where the smallest friend does the biggest job. After reading, you can retell the story, use its new words, and tell its lesson.
items.title: The Lion and the Clever Mouse

items.summary: Pip is a little rabbit who cannot sleep because the night is dark. Follow Pip from the burrow to the woods, where a lamp goes out and something wonderful appears. After reading this story you can tell it back to someone, name the words inside it, and share the small lesson it carries.
items.title: The Little Rabbit Who Was Afraid of the Dark

items.summary: A small seed falls into the dark soil and waits. Follow it through the rain, the sun and the seasons until it becomes a tree with birds in its branches. After reading, you can retell the story, use its new words, and explain its lesson about patience and care.
items.title: A Tiny Seed's Big Adventure

items.summary: One person can now direct a team of AI agents that research, write, code and check each other's work. This article examines multi-agent automation: what it does to productivity, where quality control breaks, who is responsible for the output, and what it means to 'manage' work you did not do.
items.title: The Age of AI Agents: One Human, Many Minds

items.summary: The machine writes working code in seconds, so what remains of the programmer? This article looks at how the role is shifting: from typing code to defining problems, from knowing syntax to judging systems, and why the boundary between automation and engineering skill is moving rather than disappearing.
items.title: When AI Writes Code: What Is a Programmer Worth?

items.summary: For fifteen years, software meant screens: tap here, scroll there, learn each app's menus. This article examines the shift now underway: AI agents that operate apps on our behalf, interfaces that adapt to intent, and the end of the era in which every task required a human pressing buttons.
items.title: The Future of Mobile Apps: When AI Uses Software for Us

items.summary: Short videos, endless feeds and constant notifications have trained a generation to consume content in seconds. This article examines what fragmented attention does to thinking, why deep focus is becoming rare, and how to rebuild the patience that hard ideas require.
items.title: The Death of Deep Attention

items.summary: A headache searched online becomes a brain tumor within three clicks. This article explains cyberchondria: how self-diagnosis fuels health anxiety, why scary results rise to the top of search pages, how the nocebo effect turns information into symptoms, and how to use medical information without being used by it.
items.title: Cyberchondria: When Every Symptom Becomes a Disease

items.summary: The easier it is to find an answer, the more people believe they knew it all along. This article explains the illusion of knowledge: how search engines and AI feed the Dunning–Kruger effect, why confirmation bias feels like being right, and how to tell the difference between having information and having understanding.
items.title: The Illusion of Knowledge: Why Easy Answers Feel Like Truth

items.summary: The average person meets more information in a day than a medieval farmer met in a year. This article explains what information overload does to understanding, why more facts can produce less knowledge, and how to turn an endless feed into a small set of things you actually know.
items.title: Information Overload: When Knowing Too Much Means Understanding Too Little

items.summary: Working from another country is now possible for tens of millions of people, but it is governed by visa rules, tax rules and the cost of daily life. After reading this you can tell a genuine digital nomad from a tourist working online, check what you must do before you move, and pick a city that fits your work and your budget.
items.title: Digital Nomads: Working From Anywhere

items.summary: Moving to a new country changes small things before big ones: greetings, meals, punctuality, silence. After reading this you can name what is surprising you, tell a personal habit from a local rule, and handle the first weeks without assuming that your way is the correct one.
items.title: Culture Shock: Things That Surprise People Abroad

items.summary: An anti-lock braking system is often taken as a promise that the car always stops in the same distance. It is not. After reading this you can describe how the system works, explain where it does not help, choose between threshold braking, progressive braking and engine braking, brake well with or without ABS, and say what to do when the warning light comes on.
items.title: ABS Is Not the Absolute Truth: The Limits of Anti-Lock Braking

items.summary: Washing machines, dishwashers and ovens are labelled in pictures so they can be used in any country. After reading this you can name the common symbols, choose the right programme and temperature, understand the salt, detergent and rinse aid symbols, and work a machine you have never used before.
items.title: Understanding Household Appliance Symbols

items.summary: A breakdown is a conversation you will have while standing on a hard shoulder, so the words matter. After reading this you can make the scene safe, describe the fault in a way that gets the right help sent, say what you need, and look after the people around you until someone arrives.
items.title: What to Say When Your Car Breaks Down

items.summary: A food label tells you three things: what is inside, how much of it there is, and how long it is safe. After reading this you can read any label in any country, tell a use-by date from a best-before date, and decide at the shelf whether a product is worth buying.
items.title: Reading Food Labels and Expiration Dates

items.summary: A pump moves water, and a pump that moves water can also move current. After reading this article you can name the parts of a pump installation, explain where the leakage comes from, say how current reaches a person through wet ground, compare the six protections that guard the circuit, run a safe check on a pump, and give the right instructions in the first minutes after a shock.
items.title: Water Pumps and the Risk of Electric Leakage

items.summary: A water heater is a metal tank full of water with electricity inside it. After reading this article you can describe how a fault current reaches a person, name the parts that protect you, do the right things in the first minutes after a shock, describe the fault to a technician, and keep the appliance safe between services.
items.title: Water Heaters and the Electrocution Risk

items.summary: Bảo walks into a green valley where dinosaurs still walk, and finds something small under a big leaf. Follow her past the ferns, the giant footprints and the warm nests. After reading, you can retell the journey, use five new dinosaur words in your own sentences, and explain why she left the bone in the ground.
items.title: A Journey Through Dinosaur Land

items.summary: A boy finds an old green door in the garden wall and opens it into a garden that should not exist. Follow him past the ivy, through the hidden garden and to the surprise waiting at the end. After reading, you can retell the adventure, use five new garden words in your own sentences, and explain why he keeps the door a secret.
items.title: The Secret Door in the Garden

items.summary: Tuấn finds an old map in his grandmother's attic and walks across the hill to look for buried treasure. Follow him through three clues, a compass with a shaky needle and a long afternoon of digging. After reading, you can retell the hunt, use five new explorer words in your own sentences, and say what the real treasure was.
items.title: The Little Explorer and the Hidden Treasure

items.summary: A small robot called Bit leaves the workshop to find a friend, and nothing goes the way it planned. Follow him through the street, the rain and the park at night. After reading, you can retell the adventure, use five new robot words in your own sentences, and explain how Bit finally made a friend.
items.title: The Robot Who Wanted a Friend

items.summary: A girl puts on her diving mask and swims down to the coral reef for the very first time. Follow her through the shallow water, the dark blue middle and the reef at the bottom. After reading, you can retell the adventure, use five new sea words in your own sentences, and explain why you should never touch a living coral.
items.title: My First Adventure Under the Sea

items.summary: Butterflies do not arrive in the world as butterflies. They start as eggs and change their whole shape. After reading this, you can name the four stages of a butterfly, tell a caterpillar from a chrysalis, and help a butterfly grow in your garden without hurting it.
items.title: How Butterflies Grow and Change

items.summary: Every animal has its own table, and its table decides where it lives and what it does. After reading this, you can sort animals into plant-eaters, meat-eaters and mixed-eaters, watch for the signs that tell you what an animal eats, and explain why plants and animals depend on each other.
items.title: What Do Animals Eat?

items.summary: A farm is a busy place where animals live, work and eat. After reading this you can name the animals you will meet on a farm, use the words farmers use every day, and visit a farm without frightening anybody.
items.title: Meet the Animals on the Farm

items.summary: Insects are small, but they are everywhere and they do enormous work. After reading this, you can spot an insect by its three body parts and six legs, learn what insects do for us, and watch them closely without hurting them.
items.title: The Wonderful World of Insects

items.summary: The ocean covers most of our planet, and every part of it is full of life. After reading this you can name the animals that live in each zone of the sea, use the words scientists use for them, and stay safe when you visit the beach.
items.title: Life Under the Ocean

items.summary: A pet is an animal that lives with you and depends on you every day. After reading this, you can tell what different pets need, feed and care for one properly, and know the safety rules that keep both you and the animal well.
items.title: Pets and How to Care for Them

items.summary: Bedtime is a routine, and a routine is a set of small steps you repeat every night. After reading this you can get ready for bed in the right order, say the bedtime words, talk with your family before sleep, and calm down when you cannot fall asleep.
items.title: Getting Ready for Bedtime

items.summary: A friend at school is someone you meet, talk to, and play with again and again. After reading this you can say hello to a new child, join a game, find something you both like, and keep a new friendship going.
items.title: Making Friends at School
